HEREDITARY AND EVOLUTION

HEREDITARY

Heredity and Variation

Heredity

  • Heredity is the biological process through which traits or characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through genes. It is responsible for transmission of physical, behavioural, and physiological traits, such as eye colour, blood group, and certain genetic disorders.
  • The basic unit of heredity is the gene, which is made up of DNA.

Variation

  • It refers to the differences in traits or characteristics among individuals within a species. These differences can be caused by genetic variations or environmental factors that influence how genes are expressed.
  • Variation is necessary for survival of a species (it provides the raw material for natural selection).
  • It is seen more in sexual organisms than asexual organisms (as only a single parent involved in asexual reproduction).

Genetic Traits

  • A genetic trait is a characteristic or feature of an organism that is determined by genes and can be passed down from one generation to the next.
  • Traits can be determined by genes, environmental factors or by a combination of both.
  • Traits can be qualitative (such as eye color) or quantitative (such as height or blood pressure).

Types of Traits:

  1. 1. Acquired Traits: Characteristics that develop in an organism during its lifetime as a result of environmental influences rather than genetics. E.g. Teaching, riding bike, etc.
  2. 2. Inherited Traits: Characteristics or quality that is passed down from parents to their offspring through DNA. E.g. Eye colour, blood group, etc.

Alleles

  • Alleles are alternate forms of genes, or DNA sequence, that occur at the same location on a chromosome. Alleles control the same trait, but they can produce different effects.

Types of Alleles:

  1. 1. Dominant Traits: Trait that is expressed out when one or both alleles are dominant.
  2. 2. Recessive Traits: Trait that is expressed out when both the alleles are recessive.

GREGOR MENDEL'S EXPERIMENT

  • Gregor Johan Mendel is known as "Father of Genetics". He conducted experiments of Inheritance traits in Pea Plant (Pisum sativum).

Reasons for Choosing a Pea Plant

  • It is easier to grow.
  • It has short life cycle.
  • It can be self-pollinated or cross-pollinated by hand.
  • Different traits were easily observable.
  • Many offsprings of pure pea plant can be easily obtained through self-pollination.

Three Laws of Inheritance (proposed by Gregor Mendel)

  1. 1. 1st Law (Law of Dominance): It stated that when parents with contrasting traits are crossed, only the dominant trait will appear in the offsprings.
  2. 2. 2nd Law (Law of Segregation): It stated that during the formation of gametes, the pairs of gene variants, or alleles are separated from each other. Each gamete receives one allele.
  3. 3. 3rd Law (Law of Independent Assortment): It stated that during gamete formation, alleles of two (or more) different genes get sorted into gametes independently of one another.

Monohybrid Cross

  • A monohybrid cross is a genetic experiment that studies how a single trait is passed from parents to their offspring. It involves crossing two organisms that differ in one trait. E.g. A cross between a tall pea plant and a short (dwarf) pea plant.

Monohybrid cross diagram (Tall Plant × Dwarf Plant):

  • Parental Generation: TT × tt
  • F1 Generation: All are Tt (Tall)
  • F1 × F1 selfing
  • F2 Generation: 1:2:1 genotype ratio (TT : Tt : tt); 3:1 phenotype ratio (Tall : Dwarf)
  • Punnett Square: T (TT, Tt); t (Tt, tt)
  • TT: Dominant trait
  • tt: Recessive trait

Observation

  • In the first generation Mendel found that all the offspring shared one feature, which he called dominant trait (they were all tall), and did not display any recessive trait.
  • When the first-generation plants were self-fertilized, the second generation showed the reappearance of the recessive trait in about 1 out of every 4 plants. This resulted in a 3:1 ratio, with three plants showing the dominant trait for every one showing the recessive trait.

HEREDITARY AND EVOLUTION

Dihybrid Cross

  • A dihybrid cross is a genetic cross involving two different traits, each with two contrasting alleles, where both parents are heterozygous for both traits. E.g. A cross between a seed shape (round vs. wrinkled) and seed color (yellow vs. green).

Dihybrid cross diagram (Round & Yellow Shape × Wrinkled & Green Shape):

  • P Generation: YYRR × yyrr
  • F1 Generation: YyRr (Phenotype: Round & Yellow)
  • Gametes from heterozygous parent: YR, Yr, yR, yr
  • F2 Generation: 9:3:3:1 Phenotype ratio
  • YYRR: Dominant trait
  • yyrr: Recessive trait

Observation

  • In the first generation of the dihybrid cross, Mendel found that all the offspring showed both dominant traits (round and yellow seeds), with no sign of the recessive traits (wrinkled and green).
  • When these first-generation plants were self-fertilized, the second generation showed new combinations of traits. Mendel observed four types of offspring → some showed one dominant and one recessive trait.
  • This resulted in a 9:3:3:1 ratio, with nine showing both dominant traits, three showing one dominant (YR) and three recessive trait (yR), another three showing the other combination (Yr), and one showing both recessive traits (yr).

Homologous Organ and Analogous Organ

Homologous OrganAnalogous Organ
They are organs that have the same structure but different function and are inherited from an common ancestorThey are organs of different species that have different anatomical structure but perform similar functions

SKELETAL SYSTEM

  • The skeletal system is the body's framework, providing support, protection, and allowing for movement. It comprises bones, cartilage, and ligaments, and is divided into the axial and appendicular skeletons.

Appendicular Skeleton

  • It provides support and leverage for limb movement; facilitates locomotion; and includes bones that are primarily involved in movement. E.g. bones in shoulder, pelvis, limbs, etc.
  • Bones in adult human beings: 206
  • Bones in children: 300
  • Total Axial bones: 80
  • Total Appendicular bones: 126

Axial Skeleton

  • It protects the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs; supports the head, neck, and body; and provides a rigid framework for muscle attachment. E.g. Bones in head, neck, back including skeleton etc.

Axial Skeleton — Atlas bone

  • The first cervical vertebra (C1); it supports the skull and pivots with the Axis (C2), enabling the "no" head-shaking motion.

Bones in Spinal Cord

  • Adults only have 26 bones.
  • Cervical: 7 vertebrae
  • Thoracic: 12 vertebrae
  • Lumbar: 5 vertebrae
  • Sacral: 5 vertebrae (fuse to form 1 sacrum)
  • Coccygeal: 4 vertebrae (fuse to form 1 coccyx (tailbone))

Sternum

  • Central part of the chest.
  • It is connected to ribs via cartilage.

Bones in Rib Cage

  • Total: 24 + 1 (sternum) = 25

Joint

  • A joint is a point or location where two or more bones meet, allowing for movement. Joints are also called articulations, and they are essential for flexibility and mobility in the skeletal system.

Joints and its Types

  1. 1. Synovial Joint: These joints have a fluid-filled cavity between the bones, allowing for a wide range of motion. E.g. knee, elbow, and shoulder.
  2. 2. Fibrous Joint: These joints connect bones with dense connective tissue, allowing for little to no movement. E.g. Sutures in the skull and the connection between teeth and the jawbone.
  3. 3. Cartilaginous Joint: In these joints, bones are connected by cartilage, allowing for slight movement. E.g. Joints between vertebrae and the connection between ribs and the sternum.

Teeth and its Structure

TOOTH ANATOMY (Crown, Neck, Root, Enamel, Dentin, Pulp Cavity, Gums (Gingiva), Root Canal, Bone, Cement, Nerve and Blood Vessels)

Enamel

  • Hardest part of the body (made of Calcium phosphate).
  • → Total adult teeth: 32 permanent teeth (16 in upper jaw + 16 in lower jaw including wisdom teeth)
  • Incisors: 4 → They are used for biting and cutting of food.
  • Canine: 2 → They are used for tearing of food.
  • Premolars: 4 → They are used in grinding of food.
  • Molars: 6 → They are used for chewing and crushing of food.

Dental Formula

2, 1, 2, 3 = I, C, P, M → Adults

2, 1, 2, 3 = I, C, P, M

2, 1, 0, 2 = I, C, P, M → Children

2, 1, 0, 2 = I, C, P, M

  • Total: 20 (milk teeth)

In children there are no premolars.

Sex Determination

  • Sex determination is the biological system that decides whether an individual organism will develop as male or female. It is based on genetic, chromosomal, environmental, or a combination of factors.

In humans, there are 23 pairs of chromosomes:

  • → 22 pairs are autosomics
  • → 1 pair is the sex chromosomes

Sex Chromosomes in Humans

  • Females: Have XX chromosomes.
  • Males: Have XY chromosomes.

Who Determines the Sex of the Baby?

  • The father's sperm determines the child's sex.
  • The mother's ovum always carries an X chromosome.

The sperm may carry either:

  • X chromosome → XX = Female child
  • Y chromosome → XY = Male child
